column76: Fish were sampled throughout each calendar season from the Colwater River in Quitman County, Mississippi. Fish were transported to the University of Mississippi and housed in similar conditions to the ones they were acclimated to in the field. Field temperatures (to which the fish were acclimated) were (from spring to winter): 21.3, 27.3, 16.2, and 6.7°C. In the lab, four temperatures and photoperiods were used for each season: 20°C & 12L:12D (spring); 27°C & 15L:9D (summer); 17°C & 12L:12:d (fall); 10°C & 10L:14D (winter). Fish were tested 1-4 days after capture. Specifically (again from spring to winter), the groups of fish were held for: 3.6, 1.4, 3.1, and 2.6 days. Swimming trials were conducted in a swim tunnel respirometer. Before testing, fish were allowed a 15-20 hour habituation period to the swim tunnel, during which the water velocity in the tunnel was 5 cm/s. During the swim experiment, overhead lighting in the swimming tunnel room remained on until the fish fatigued; therefore, some individuals experienced an additional 2-3 h of light. A variation of the standard critical swimming speed protocol described by Brett (1964) was applied. That is, a 30-minute rest period was allowed between each velocity increment such that the respirometer could be replenished with oxygen. The modified protocol began at a water velocity of 10 cm/s, followed by stepwise increases of 10 cm/s after successful completion of each bout. These increases continued until the fish fatigued. Each buffalo was only tested once. Ucrit was calculated as outlined by Brett (1964): ucrit = U1 + (U2)(t1/t2). VO2s were monitored for 1 hour at each speed increment until the fish fatigued. Active metablolic rates were measured, and standard metabolic rates were estimed by extrapolating the relationship between speed and VO2 to zero activity/zero swim speed.

column107: Smallmouth buffalo were sampled throughout each calendar season from Jan. 19, 1995 to Feb. 5, 1996. They were collected and transported 97 km to the University of Mississippi in a tank filled with river water. In the lab, they were transferred to dechlorinated tap water. Fish were tested 1-4 d after capture and were not fed in captivity. Stomachs were not examined to confirm a post-aborptive state, but time expired between capture and experimentation for all fish was a minimum of 20 h. An acclimitaization protocol similar to that of Facey and Grossman (1990) were used. That is, fish were held at conditions (seasonal temperature and photoperiod) similar to natural conditions from which they were removed. Thus, spring, summer, fall, and winter buffalo were held and tested under the following temperature and photoperiod regimes, respectively: 20°C & 12L:12D; 27°C & 15L:9D; 17°C & 12L:12:d; 10°C & 10L:14D.

Before testing, fish were allowed a 15-20 hour habituation period to the swim tunnel, during which the water velocity in the tunnel was 5 cm/s. During the swim experiment, overhead lighting in the swimming tunnel room remained on until the fish fatigued; therefore, some individuals experienced an additional 2-3 h of light. A variation of the standard critical swimming speed protocol described by Brett (1964) was applied. That is, a 30-minute rest period was allowed between each velocity increment such that the respirometer could be replenished with oxygen. column76: Mating and swimming trials were conducted at 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, and 38°C, with individual fish used for only one performance measure (mating or swimming) at one temperature. Experimental fish were exposed to an acute change in temperature at a rate that did not exceed 4°C/h. Swimming/mating performance was assessed at least 10 min (no more than 1h) after the test temperature was reached to ensure that the animals had equilibrated with the aquarium temperature. Mating behaviour of each male was assessed during a 10-min observation period. During this time, the male was in an aquarium containing six mature females. Separate groups of sex female G holbrooki with total body lengths of 3.7 -- 4.5 cm were selected for each male observation period. Groups of six were chosen to ensure that females were not stressed and no single female was continuously harassed. Only nonvirgin females that had not given birth during the previous 5 days were used, since postpartum females may affect male behaviour. Before observations, females were allowed to settle in the observation tank for 30 minutes prior to the introduction of the male fish. Males were randomly selected from host tanks. The observation period was started when the male first began to follow one of the females. During the observation period, several mating behaviours were recorded and entered into the Behavioural software program ETHOM 1.0. Recorded variables were: total time each male spent following all females combined, and the total number of unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Total # of mating attempts included both unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Burst swimming performance was assessed by filming at least five startle responses for each individual with a high-speed digital camera. Swimming responses were elicited by tapping the side of the tank. Swimming sequences were filmed by recording the image at an angle of 90° below the glass-bottomed aquarium. The Redlake software packaged was used for analysis of the startle responses. Sequences were replayed frame by frame and the centre region of the head was digitized. The distance moved by individual fish between each successive frame for each startle response sequence was determined, followed by  instantaneous measures of velocity. The fastest of the swimming sequences analysed for each individual was used as a measure of its maximum burst swimming performance. Effects of temperature on the speeds of males during copulation attempts were also examined: individual males were placed into the same filming arena with two adult females, and their mating behaviour was recorded. Distance moved by each male between each frame during mating attempts was determined. Velocity measurements were based on the digitization of the centre point of the head for each male. Maximal approach speed was calculated bu taking the maximum instantaneous speed recorded during each sequence. For these swimming trials, 10 fish were observed at each temperature (n = 70).

column76: Mating and swimming trials were conducted at 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, and 38°C, with individual fish used for only one performance measure (mating or swimming) at one temperature. Experimental fish were exposed to an acute change in temperature at a rate that did not exceed 4°C/h. Swimming/mating performance was assessed at least 10 min (no more than 1h) after the test temperature was reached to ensure that the animals had equilibrated with the aquarium temperature. Mating behaviour of each male was assessed during a 10-min observation period. During this time, the male was in an aquarium containing six mature females. Separate groups of sex female G holbrooki with total body lengths of 3.7 -- 4.5 cm were selected for each male observation period. Groups of six were chosen to ensure that females were not stressed and no single female was continuously harassed. Only nonvirgin females that had not given birth during the previous 5 days were used, since postpartum females may affect male behaviour. Before observations, females were allowed to settle in the observation tank for 30 minutes prior to the introduction of the male fish. Males were randomly selected from host tanks. The observation period was started when the male first began to follow one of the females. During the observation period, several mating behaviours were recorded and entered into the Behavioural software program ETHOM 1.0. Recorded variables were: total time each male spent following all females combined, and the total number of unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Total # of mating attempts included both unsuccessful mating attempts and successful copulations. Burst swimming performance was assessed by filming at least five startle responses for each individual with a high-speed digital camera. Swimming responses were elicited by tapping the side of the tank. Swimming sequences were filmed by recording the image at an angle of 90° below the glass-bottomed aquarium. The Redlake software packaged was used for analysis of the startle responses. Sequences were replayed frame by frame and the centre region of the head was digitized. The distance moved by individual fish between each successive frame for each startle response sequence was determined, followed by  instantaneous measures of velocity. The fastest of the swimming sequences analysed for each individual was used as a measure of its maximum burst swimming performance. Effects of temperature on the speeds of males during copulation attempts were also examined: individual males were placed into the same filming arena with two adult females, and their mating behaviour was recorded. Distance moved by each male between each frame during mating attempts was determined. Velocity measurements were based on the digitization of the centre point of the head for each male. Maximal approach speed was calculated bu taking the maximum instantaneous speed recorded during each sequence. For these swimming trials, 10 fish were observed at each temperature (n = 70).

column76: Sixty G. brasiliensis (n = 4 per experimental unit) were randomly allocated to the experimental treatments from an initial temperature of 20°C. **Each treatment was done in 3 replicates (so sample size for each temperature = 3 x 4 = 12). The fish were starved for 24 hours before receiving snails as prey (these snails {P. canaliculata} were collected from localities with rice paddies). column76: Fish were collected in fall 1990 and reared at 7°C for several months prior to the experiment. The fish were divided into six groups with 33 immature fish per group. The rearing experiment lasted for 189 days. Temps of each group were: 2.4, 4.6, 7.0, 9.8, 12.6, and 15.1°C. A natural photoperiod was maintained. The halibut were tagged with numbered spaghetti tags to allow growth rate of individual fish to be calculated. The fish were weighed every 3 months and were not fed for 3 days prior to weighing, and specific growth rates & growth efficiencies were calculated.
column102: This paper comprises of 3 experiments: A, B, and C, but only C dealt with wild fish. I extracted the data on the hatchery-reared fish but moved it to the "Notes tab".
column107: The experiments were carried out indoors. The seawater supply was obtained from a well where water was 7°C and salinity 32 per mille. In the growth trials, water exchange was regulated so that the O2 concentration was always above 6 mg/L. Temperatures were adjusted by approximately 1°C/day until target temperatures were reached. This study did three experiments: two on hatchery-reared fish, one on wild fish. Only the latter is present here. The fish had been collected in Faxaflói (a large bay in southwest Iceland) in autumn of 1990. These fish were reared at 7°C for several months prior to the experiment. This experiment lasted 189 days (March 5, 1991 -- September 10, 1991). They were fed once a day on either chopped herring or on whole capelin. The halibut were tagged with numbered spaghetti tags to allow growth rate of individual fish to be calculated. These fish were weighed every 3 months and were not fed 3 days prior to weighing.

column76: Swimming experiments were carried out at 14, 18, 22, 26 and 30°C in a sealable, recirculating flume. Ambient temperature in the room housing the flume was 22°C. Swimming experiments were carried out at all temperatures in air saturated water, and additionally at 30°C with the dissolved oxygen content elevated to 12.0 mg/L by bubbling 100% oxygen into the water via an air stone. The large volume of water in the flume meant that rapid temperature changes could not be applied using the heaters or chiller. Rates of temperature change were limited to approximately 1°C per hour. Consequently fish could not be exposed to an instantaneous temperature change while in the flume. Exposure to slow temperature changes was undesirable, as this had the potential to allow for at least partial acclimation to temperatures other than Ta. Video sequences were recorded using a Sony HDR HC-3 camcorder at a frame rate of 120 Hz at speeds ranging from 8.4 to a maximum of 51.1·cm·s–1 (0.44–2.68·l·s–1), the upper limit varying with water temperature. Under each set of conditions speed was increased from 8.4·cm·s–1 (0.44·l·s–1) in approximately 4·cm·s–1 (0.21·l·s–1) increments. At each speed the fish was allowed to swim for 5·min before video recording was started. The same group of fish was used for measurements of maximal swimming performance. A protocol involving incremental changes in swimming speed was used to establish Umax using the same group of fish for which kinematic data were obtained. Starting at 8.4·cm·s–1, speed was increased in 4·cm·s–1 increments and maintained at a given level for 10·min between increments. Speed increases continued until the fish could no longer maintain position in the flume. Umax (in cm·s–1)=Ufin+4(T/Tint), where Ufin (in cm·s–1) was the speed of the final interval at which steady swimming could be maintained and TInt was the time interval between speed increments. This test was not equivalent to a critical swimming speed (Ucrit) test. The aim was to determine maximal aerobically supported performance in a similar manner to Claireaux et al. (Claireaux et al., 2006).

column76: About 300 mackerels (18.29 +/- cm FL) were obtained. They were seasonally separated in four groups and acclimated at different water temperatures (10, 15, 18, and 22°C) for over a week. The fish group of 10°C was obtained in winter (Dec. to Feb.); the group of 15 was collected in sprin (March to May); the group of 18 in autumn (Sept. to Nov.); the group of 22°C was collected in summer (June to Aug.). The tail beat frequency increase following the swimming speed level was observed in the swimming channel of a flume tank (West Japan Fluid Engineering Laboratory, PT-70). The water temperature in the flume tank was maintained at the desired temperature in each fish group (10, 15, 18 and 22 ºC). Each individual was randomly selected and placed in the swimming channel and adapted for 10 minutes to low flow speed (12.4 cm/s) conditions. The tail beat frequency was recorded using a video camera during swimming exercise at various levels of swimming speed, i.e. 20.4, 39.3, 55.4, 74.3, 93.1, 112.0, 128.1, 147.0 and 160.4 cm s-1, being equal to 1.1, 2.1, 3.0, 4.1, 5.1, 6.1, 7.0, 8.0 and 8.8 FL s-1, respectively. The tail beat frequency of the individual fish at each swimming speed was counted at the slow-motion mode of the video timer. Muscle contraction times were measured using a pair of needles punctured at dorsal muscle of fish body. Minimum muscle contraction time (Tm) data at given temperatures yield maximum tail frequency (Fmax), through an equation as Fmax = 1/2 Tm (Wardle 1975). The maximum swimming speed (Umax) was estimated by a linear regression between tail beat frequency (F) and maximum swimming speed (U, FL s-1) at each temperature, Umax = a + b F.

column76: Fish remained in holding tanks to recover for >5 days prior to trials and were acclimated to new experimental temperatures by changing their holding tanks by <2C per day. Experiments with the first group of fish were performed at 6, 12, and 18C in sequential order, with temperature acclimation periods of >5 days prior. The second group of fish completed only 24C trials. In each group of fish, two individuals were untagged due to tag number limitations, generating swimming data without acceleration. Smallmouth bass were transferred individually into a 185-L swim tunnel respirometer. Accelerometer transmitter outputs were measured using a VR100 manual receiver (InnovaSea). Fish were introduced to the swimming portion, the chamber was sealed, and fish were given 5 min to rest. A practice swim was then initiated, beginning with a water flow speed of 10 cm s1, increasing over 3 min to 50 cm s1, and maintaining for 12 min with the chamber sealed. The speed was then reduced to 10 cm s1, and the chamber was flushed with fresh water for 45 min to allow oxygen to replenish and fish to recover. The experimental swimming protocol was then initiated using a ramp-Ucrit design where fish were exposed to swimming speeds starting at 40 cm s1, in 10-cm s1 increments, with 20 min at each speed. When fish did not swim to maintain position in the tunnel, the back grid was electrified to encourage swimming. Three successive shocks with <5 s of resumed swimming in between was the endpoint for each trial, and the time to end was recorded to calculate critical swimming speed. At the end of each experimental day, background respiration was measured in the tunnel by sealing the system for 1 h at 10 cm/s.
column88: Ucrit = Vf + [(T/t)(dV)], where Vf is the last full speed completed, T is the duration at final increment, t is the duration at each speed increment, and dV is the speed increment.

column76: For the determination of Ucrit, water velocity was increased stepwise by 0.3 BL s1 every 10 min, from a starting velocity of 1 BL s1, until the fish fatigued. A swimming interval of 10 min was chosen based on a synthesis of literature showing that 10 min is an appropriate interval for Ucrit determination (Jones 1971; Beamish 1980; Hammer 1995). When fish failed to maintain swim performance, water velocity was decreased to 0 to allow the fish to come off of the screen and resume swimming. Velocity was then increased to the velocity of failure within 10s. Final fatigue was established when the fish fell against the back screen three consecutive times.

column76: The body length of each test fish was measured and placed into the swim chamber to adapt to experimental conditions at 0.5 BL/s for 2 h before the test began (Jain et al. 1997). The initial velocity was 1BL/s, and velocity was increased by increments in 1BL/s at 30-min intervals (20-min DO measurement, 5-min flushing with air-saturated water and 5-min equilibration). The temperature and the DO were measured at 10-min intervals until the fish was fatigued (the fish ceases swimming and rests against the grid for 20 s (Lee et al. 2003a). (2010)). Fish were individually transferred into the swim tunnel and were allowed to recover for 1 h at a water velocity of 6 cm s-1 (approximately 1 BL s-1, where BL denotes body lengths). The flow of aerated water through the respirometer was maintained continuously during this recovery period. The water temperature in the swimming chamber was controlled within ±0.2 C using a water bath connected to a stainless steel heat exchanger. The water velocity in the swim tunnel was then steadily increased at a rate of 0.1667 cm s-2 (10 cm s-1 min-1). The water was accelerated at this rate until the fish were exhausted. Fatigue was defined as the failure of the fish to move away from the rear honeycomb screen of the swimming chamber for 20 s (Lee et al. 2003a, b).

column76: Fertilized trout eggs were collected from four cutthroat trout populations native to Colorado during peak spawning activity in June of 2018. Each female was stripped into a dry bowl then fertilized with milt from a single male. Fry from all populations were reared under common conditions. Growth trials were conducted by testing each population with three replicates at 6 different temperature treatments. For each population, 18 lots of 15 fish, each representing an even mix of each of the remaining families, were isolated at 126-day post hatch. Target temperatures for each system were 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, and 26 ◦C, maintained with either 800 or 1500 W submersible titanium aquarium heaters with automatic temperature controllers. With different populations reaching the 126-day post-hatch start threshold at different times, it was impossible to acclimate fish by increasing 1 ◦C each day until target temperatures were reached, as in other studies. Accordingly, we acclimated fish by moving their tanks through the temperature ladder provided by the grow-out system baths. For example, fish that were destined to spend 21 days at 23 ◦C were moved from the 13 ◦C round rearing tanks to three 14 ◦C chambers three days prior to the experiment, then to the 17 ◦Cbathtwo days prior, followed by the 20 ◦C bath the day before, reaching the target temperature of 23 ◦C on Day 0. With each transition, the volume of water in the tank was replaced with new (3 ◦C warmer) water over an 18 min period, which served as the tempering phase each day.

column76: For each species, fish were initially measured and stocked into experimental tanks at a density of three individuals/tank. The size range of fish used in the experiments was purposely restricted to focus on the effects of temperature rather than size-dependent growth. After establishment of experimental groups, temperatures were adjusted to treatment temperatures (0, 5, 9, and 16 °C) at a rate of 1.5 °C per day. Replicate tanks (n = 2) of each temperature treatment (n = 4) were assigned for each species (n = 4) to comprise a total of 32 tanks. At week 2 following the acclimation period, fish were weighed to the nearest 0.01 g (wet mass) and measured to the nearest 1 mm (SL) to establish ‘time 0’ for the growth experiment. After measurement, all fish were returned to their original tank and remeasured in the same manner at week 4 (period week 2–week 4) and again at week 6 (period week 4week 6) of the experiment to assess growth. At the end of the experiment, an additional 20 °C trial was conducted for species able to survive and maintain growth at 16 °C during the initial experiment. Fish used for the 20 °C trial were sourced from general holding tanks and had not been used in the original growth experiment. Specific growth rates based on mass of juvenile fish were determined. SGR = 100 - (e^g - 1), where g = ln(WW2) - ln(WW1)/ (t2 - t1). The same approach was used to calculate mean tank growth based on total tank biomass. Notable deviations in the two growth metrics can be an indicator of growth suppression due to social interactions within the tank.

column107: Live juvenile fish of similar size were collected by either fyke net (Arctic and saffron cod), beach seine (Pacific cod), or lift net (walleye pollock) and shipped from a variety of locations to Newport, OR in 2012 (see Table 1 for details). Apparent satiation was determined as the point where excess food remained in the tank 1 h after feeding. Daily feedings were conducted in this manner across the entire acclimation and experimental period. Lights were maintained on a 12:12 light/dark photoperiod for all experiments. Tanks were checked daily for mortalities, and dead fish were removed, weighed and measured.

column76: Burbot were caught by trap-nets in Lake P ̈ aij ̈ anne (central Finland) during February–March spawning season. The feeding experiment was performed at four temperatures 2.4, 5.1, 10.8, and 23.4C(S:D:0:49C). Fish were exposed to the natural seasonal water temperature variation between experiments to maximise their acclimation to higher water temperatures during spring and summer. The mean weight of burbot used in the experiment was 296 g .S:D: 48 g; range D 104–353 g; n D 66/ and the mean length 324 mm .S:D:  22 mm; range D 280–380 mm; n D 66/. Burbot .n D 24 initially at each temperature) were randomly selected for the experiment and placed in circular cages .r D 250 mm, h D 750 mm) and then allowed to recover from the handling stress and acclimate to the test environment for 8–14 d (one fish per cage). They were fed vendace at 1–3 d intervals during the acclimation period. During the experiments, the burbot were fed freshly thawed vendace weighing 2.5–3.5 g. For each experiment the average weight of 260 vendace was calculated .mean D 3:02 g, s:d: D 0:11 g) and they were then frozen and stored at −25C. Burbot were fed once a day with 10 whole vendace. After 10 min any vendace remaining in the cage was removed. The number of vendace consumed was recorded and the weight of the meal estimated by multiplying the number of vendace eaten by average weight of vendace in the batch. Burbot that were ill or did not eat were removed from the experiment and the results are based only on data from the healthy animals. Burbot were not reused in the experiment. The total duration of experiments was 21 d at 2.4C, 16 d at 5.1C and 14 d at 10.8C and 23.4C. Mean daily food intake (MDI) values were calculated for each fish (g d−1). Food amounts were also related to burbot weight (RDI, g g−1 d−1) to analyse the effect of burbot size on food intake at different temperatures.

column76: One month before the start of the experiments, mature females were placed in a 400 l aquarium and maintained under standard conditions (food: ad libitum and temp 30°C). The fish were not fed for two days prior to the start of the experiment and on the last day of the experiment, so that gut contents would not affect true body weights. The experiments were run for 30 days. Individual treatments in the experiment were 18, 20, 23, 25 & 27 °C. Upon termination of the experiments, the fish were sacrificed with an overdose of MS-222 (tricaine methane sulfonate) and were weighed with and without their ovaries. Ovary weight was calculated as the difference between the two weights (this method is preferable for determining the weight of small ovaries). The gonado-somatic index (GSI = gonad weight/bodyweight  100) was calculated for each fish and group averages were calculated for each treatment.

Illumination was provided by standard fluorescent bulbs in overhead fixtures. All experiments were carried out in aquaria equipped with under-gravel filters and aeration. column76: The spontaneous swimming speeds of randomly chosen fish were analysed using Logger Pro v.3.8.6 (Vernier software, Beaverton, OR, USA). In short, based on the dorsal view of the test subject, the x and y coordinates of the tip of the snout and the tip of the caudal fin was manually marked on the first frame. The geometric centre of one of the eyes was then marked on every 10th frame over no less than 150 frames. This provided a record of the change in the x and y coordinates over a period of no less than 5 s. The average rate of spontane ous swimming speeds (i.e. the cumulative distance swum in body length per second, bls1) was then calculated from the positional (x and y) data relative to the total length of the fish. Whenever possible, the source population of the fish (high or low latitude) was recorded based on the colour of the attached T-bar tags. Individuals that could not be identified to population level were recorded as unknown.
column102: the two different collection sites differ in mean water temperature by ca. 3 °C year round with the low-latitude region averaging 23.9 °C in winter and 29.3 °C in summer, compared to 20.8 °C and 27.0 °C in the high-latitude region.
column107: Different coloured tags were used for the two populations to allow fish from the high- and low-latitude populations to be readily distinguished. Fish from each population were then randomly distributed across eight 2000 L round tanks (120 9 150 cm, height 9 diameter) and held under a 13–11 h light–dark regime (subjected to sunrise and sunset as beginning and end of daylight). Tanks were continuously supplied with filtered seawater (salinity 34 ppt) at an initial temperature of 24°C. This temperature corresponded to the temperature ( 2 °C) recorded during field collections. After 4–5 days, the fish assigned to warmer temperatures were slowly brought to their experimental temperature of 27, 30, or 33 °C ( 0.2 °C), with increases in temperature at a maximum rate of 0.5 °C/day. All fish were held at experimental temperatures in fully oxygenated water (equivalent to 44.75, 42.61, 40.67, and 38.92 lg O2/L/mmHg respectively) for a minimum of 4 weeks before experiments began to ensure full metabolic acclimation.

column76: RMR trials began in the morning at approximately the same time throughout the experiment. Although we stopped feeding the fish 40 h prior to the experiment, our metabolic measurements were taken on growing juvenile lake trout (not on a maintenance ration) and are therefore growth-inflated metabolic rates. Flow rates were low enough so that fish were inactive (not swimming), and the chambers were narrow enough so that fish could not turn around. fish were transferred to the chambers the afternoon prior to RMR measurements allowing them 16 hrs to acclimate to their new surroundings. Fish had at least 40 hrs following their last feeding before experiments were conducted in order to remove the effect of digestion on RMR readings (Allen et al., 2016). Oxygen consumption rates were recorded for three, 5 min intervals with a 5 min flush period between each measurement to allow fresh water to enter the system and replenish the oxygen.  MMR tests were performed on two fish simultaneously (one per rtechnician) and involved measuring oxygen consumption on fish that were exhausted by implementing a chase protocol (Clark et al., 2013).Once fish were exhausted (3 to 8 min), they were quickly transferred to the respirometry chamber and the flush pump was turned off and on for eight consecutive 5 min oxygen consumption measurements over a 75 min period.  Aerobic performance was assessed by comparing the time to exhaustion and metabolic recovery of each strain (Clark et al., 2013).

raised, daily mean was 9.10 C and standard deviation was 0.98 C). Except for eyed eggs for Slate Island, all eggs were brought to Codrington as fertilized eggs. The eggs were reared in family partitioned Heath trays until hatching and were then moved to 60 L family specific tanks that were divided in two to hold two separate families (McDermid et al., 2013). The size and amount of optimum salmonid feed (Corey Nutrition Co., redericton, NB, Canada) was evaluated on a monthly basis to allow for maximum growth using the recommended feeding
guide for salmonids provided by the feed supplier. The size of the feed was adjusted to match the mean size of the fish and the amount of feed was dependent on the biomass in the tanks (mean biomass specific to the strains). The biomass was monitored closely to avoid exceeding 34 g/L to ensure maximum growth. Fish were clipped to identify families (January 2016) and pit-tagged (October 2016) to track individuals.

column76: RMR trials began in the morning at approximately the same time throughout the experiment. Although we stopped feeding the fish 40 h prior to the experiment, our metabolic measurements were taken on growing juvenile lake trout (not on a maintenance ration) and are therefore growth-inflated metabolic rates. Flow rates were low enough so that fish were inactive (not swimming), and the chambers were narrow enough so that fish could not turn around. fish were transferred to the chambers the afternoon prior to RMR measurements allowing them 16 hrs to acclimate to their new surroundings. Fish had at least 40 hrs following their last feeding before experiments were conducted in order to remove the effect of digestion on RMR readings (Allen et al., 2016). Oxygen consumption rates were recorded for three, 5 min intervals with a 5 min flush period between each measurement to allow fresh water to enter the system and replenish the oxygen.  MMR tests were performed on two fish simultaneously (one per rtechnician) and involved measuring oxygen consumption on fish that were exhausted by implementing a chase protocol (Clark et al., 2013).Once fish were exhausted (3 to 8 min), they were quickly transferred to the respirometry chamber and the flush pump was turned off and on for eight consecutive 5 min oxygen consumption measurements over a 75 min period.  Aerobic performance was assessed by comparing the time to exhaustion and metabolic recovery of each strain (Clark et al., 2013).

column76: The absorption efficiency was determined using the Conover (1966) method. For this, we determined the organic fraction of representative samples of the faeces from H. antarcticus and the diet supplied (i.e., G. antarctica). Samples of food and faeces were filtered through pre-ashed, pre-weighed, 25-mm glass fiber filters, rinsed with isotonic ammonium formate, dried to a constant weight at 80 °C, weighed, combusted at 450 °C for 3 h, and weighed again to estimate the organic and inorganic fraction contained in the food and faeces. The absorption rate was calculated as the product of the organic ingestion rate and absorption efficiency. For each fish, ingestion and absorption rates were averaged over time (n = 5) before conducting the statistical analyses

column102: netted from late september to early october at end of growing season. body metric info taken from table 1
column107: In the laboratory, fish were kept in wooden, glass-fronted, continuous-flow, holding tanks (86.5 X 46 X 30 cm; water height, 25 cm) of 99.5 L capacity. All tanks were equipped with inflows, outflows, heaters, and regulators. Tests were run at six test temperatures: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30°C. Each series was duplicated. Biomasses of fish in the tanks were equivalent at the start of the experiments: 31-42 g wet weight for year 0 and 102- 140 g for the year 2 fish. The numbers of fish per tank were 8- 10 for the smaller and 3-5 for the larger size group. Within each tank, sizes of indi- viduals were varied slightly so that the growth history of each indi- vidual could be followed; this and observing feeding were used as a means of monitoring health. (Bullheads do not exhibit the dominance hierarchy that may lead to differential growth rates in centrarchids (A. Keast, unpublished data).) Positions of the tanks were random ized. Day length was on a 12 h light : 12 h dark schedule. Kingston municipal water, dechlorinated by passage through charcoal filters, was used (67 mg CaC03/L, pH 7.2).

column102: This population was introduced in 1999 (Mitchell and Purchase 2014) from Indian Bay, NL (COSEWIC 2014). Embryos were collected on artificial (yarn, 10- to 15-cm-long threads) spawning mops (20), which were used to mimic the plant substrate that banded killifish eggs typically adhere to. The second collection took place 4h later, and therefore, embryos were known to be within the first 4 h of development. Individual embryos were fully immersed in water in Petri dishes placed in incubators at their respective temperatures, and the water was topped up daily. The majority of the embryos were collected between 27 June and 1 July (n 1⁄4 84). Because of low hatch success at the lower temperatures, we collected additional embryos (n 1⁄4 23; between 9 and 11 July) and added them evenly into the 10 and 16 C levels to increase the sample size.

column53: There are 2 recirculating systems and 4 tanks (at 4 diff temperatures) per system. There are 13 fish per tank. The fish were all individually weighed, so the results for each temperature treatment are based off of 2 x 13 = 26 observations.
column76: Fish were held in holding tanks, whose temperaures were adjusted over a period of 5 days to 17, 22, 27, and 32°C. The fish were held at these temperature for a week. Following acclimation, the fish in each tank were size sorted and the large and small individuals discarded. Thirteen fish were inidividually weighed and stocked per tank in each of the 2 recirculating systems. The fish were maintained for 8 weeks and all the fish in each tank were group weighed every other week. Feed was offered at 3% body weight (of the largest group weight) daily. The ration was increased by 5% for the second week (to reduce risk of underfeeding) and then readjusted to 3% body weight after the fish were weighed again. Eight weeks after the start of the experiment, all tanks were harvested and the fish from each tank were group weighed and then their individual weight and length were measured.

column76: Fish were removed from their acclimation tanks with a dip net and placed in a Loligo mini swim tunnel respirometer (Loligo Systems, Tjele, Denmark) containing 20 ppt water at the acclimation temperature of the fish. The tunnel was set at the lowest speed possible to minimize stratification of water oxygen concentrations but to avoid the fish actively swimming against the current. Fish were allowed 30 min to adjust to the respirometer before the onset of measurement. After the 30-min recovery time, the tunnel was sealed, and the decrease in water oxygen concentration over time, measured using NeoFox oxygen probes (Ocean Optics, Dunedin, FL) with a sampling rate of once every 15 s, was used to calculate mass- specific M ̇ O2routine, as in Sloman et al. (2008) and Fangue et al. (2009b). Fish remained quiescent during the measurement pe- riod, and the oxygen trace interval that gave a constant rate of decrease for at least 5 min and resulted in the lowest M ̇ O2 was used to calculate M ̇ O2routine. The respirometers were rinsed daily with a 75% ethanol solution, which resulted in negligible bacterial respiration (!1% of total oxygen consumption) in all trials. Note that M ̇ O2routine was measured once per fish.

column76: growth was measured using the acclimated chronic exposure methodology (Zale 1984; Selonget al. 2001; Bear et  al. 2007), modified to last 33 d instead of 60 d. The experimental design, temperature control, head tanks, and fish tanks were as described for the egg test, except that flow to each tank was increased to 50 mL/min to accommodate the increased biomass of fry. The test used Mountain White fish fry that were incubated in Ft. Collins dechlorinated municipal tap water at 4.5◦C until hatch. After hatch, the temperature was warmed to 10◦C over 12 h. At the start of each test, twenty fry were randomly allocated to each tank. Fry were 9 d posthatch in 2008 and 12 d posthatch 2009. Temperatures of the head tanks wereadjusted to target temperatures at a rate of 1◦C/d from a startingtemperature of 10◦C. The number of fry subsampled from each tank was adjusted formortality when necessary so that the number of fry remainingin each tank was constant among treatments.Subsampled frywere euthanized with 500 mg/L MS-222, blotted dry with apaper towel and weighed to 0.001 g. Fry nwere fed brine shrimp nauplii  to satiation three times a day (once a day onweekends and holidays).

column76: Conversion efficiency was calculated for fish held individually in 82 l tanks (n = 12 replicates per temper- ature) in a flow-through system during 3 wk experi- ments in 1999 (Table 1). Temperatures were ambient (mean = 12°C) when fish were introduced to tanks, and gradually increased or decreased at a rate of 2°C d–1 to the target level during the first week. Fish received either 2 or 3 mm BioDiet pellets (composition noted above) distributed from automatic feeders over a 1 h period. Pellets remaining in tanks after the feeding period were counted and removed by siphoning. The total number of pellets consumed each week by each fish was determined and the dry weight of food con- sumed calculated from previously determined rela- tionships.

column76: At the conclusion of experiments conducted in 1999, groups were randomly selected for measurement of swimming activity levels. Prior to final length and weight measurements, groups were transferred to circular (122 cm diameter), 340 l tanks filled with water of the same temperature used during growth evaluation. After a 30 min acclimation period, groups were video- taped with overhead cameras. There were 4 replicate groups from each ration/temperature treatment, with the exception of the 24°C treatment, which had only 1 tank with survivors in the high ration treatment. Each group was filmed for 1 h; no food was present during filming. Videotapes were analyzed with an image analysis system using a digitizing pen to trace the movement of individual fish. Each fish of a pair was tracked for 30 s, with 4 sets of observations at approxi- mately 10 min intervals. Due to the shallow water depth (30 cm), movement occurred primarily in the horizontal plane, justifying use of the overhead 2- dimensional video image to assess activity. The average speed of fish (body lengths s–1) moving through the tank was calculated for each interval and averaged overall for each group.

column76: Routine oxygen uptake (RMR) was measured from the decline in dissolved oxygen saturation of water within two custom-made, intermittent-flow, airtight and lightproof respirometers 8.0× 15.5×22.5 cm. Gut evacuation from repletion in B. saida took 36– 70 h at −1.5 to −0.5°C, with an average of 51 h (Hop et al., 1997). Thus, after a 48 h fasting period, a fish was transferred to each of the two respirometers, which were connected to a 32 litre, closed-circuit sump that contained two refrigerant coils attached to two programmable chillers (Fisher Isotemp 3016d; www.fisherssci.com) filled with 60% propylene glycol antifreeze. The seawater sump was continuously aerated and also held a magnetic drive pump. Water temperature was controlled by the recirculating chillers and measured to a precision of ±0.1°C (Fisher Scientific Type K digital thermometer probe). A pilot experiment that measured oxygen uptake over 47.5 h while wild-caught B. saida became accustomed to the respirometer found that RMR stabilized between 12 h and 22 h (see Fig. 2A, inset). Consequently, all RMR measurements began following an overnight acclimation of minimally 12 h. Water temperature was adjusted at a rate of 3°C h−1 to the desired acute test temperature for that experiment: 0.5, 2.0, 3.5, 5.0 and 7.5°C for the 3.5°C acclimation group, and 0.5, 2.5, 4.5, 6.5 and 8.5°C for the 1.0°C and 6.5°C acclimation groups. At the test temperature, fish were held for 1 h before measuring RMR using closed respirometry that recorded the depletion of oxygen from the water with a fibre optic oxygen meter for up to 30 min (Firesting O2, PyroScience, Aachen, Germany). This procedure was repeated 2-3 times and the lowest value was reported as RMR. Then, the fish was removed from the respirometer and placed in a ∼12 litre circular tank containing aerated water at the test temperature for exhaustive exercise. Chasing involved a 5 min period of hand chasing, gentle tail pinches and lifting until unresponsive to touch, followed by brief air exposure (Norin and Clark, 2016). The fish was returned to the respirometer and oxygen uptake measurement resumed within 30 s and continued over 5–30 min, depending on the test temperature. The maximum oxygen uptake (MMR) was calculated from the steepest 2–5% decrease in percentage water saturation, which occurred consistently at the start of recording. Water oxygen saturation never decreased below 75% saturation for any measurement. After the MMR measurement, fish were weighed, pit tagged (if newly tested) and returned to their acclimation tank. AAS was calculated as MMR −RMR and factorial aerobic scope (FAS) as MMR/RMR. Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) was measured at 0.5 and 1 h after MMR to compare the % return to initial RMR values for the 1.0°C and 6.5°C acclimated fish. Tests with the 1.0°C acclimation group used 20 fish bred at the Vancouver Aquarium with a mean mass of 59.8±2.7 g. Tests with the 3.5°C acclimation group used 19 wild fish caught in 2011 with a mean mass of 111.5±6.1 g. Tests with the 6.5°C acclimation group used 11 fish bred at the Vancouver Aquarium and 6 wild fish caught in 2012 with a mean mass of 74.1±7.6 g.

column76: Swimming performance was measured as the critical sustained swimming speed (Ucrit; Brett 1965) in an oval doughnut-shaped flume (2.32 m long # 1.10 m wide [0.32 m width of the swimming lane] # 0.70 m deep). During swimming trials, fish were individually contained in a restricted space (0.41 m long # 0.32 m wide # 0.70 m deep) within which laminar flow was approximated by a series of baffles. Unidirectional flow was produced by an electric outboard motor (Riptide RT40, Minn Kota, Mankato, MN), which was regulated with a variable DC power supply (MP3090, Powertech, Melbourne). Flow was proportional to the voltage output of the power sup- ply, and the power supply settings were calibrated using a flow probe (FP101, GlobalWater, Gold River, CA; sensitive to 0.01 m s1) so that voltage output could be related to water velocity in the restricted swimming space. The flume was situated in a temperature-controlled room, and water temperature was ad- ditionally regulated by two immersion heaters (Julabo Ther- momix, Seelbach, Germany). Fish were introduced into the flume enclosure for 10 min before experimen- tation to equilibrate body temperature to water temperature (Seebacher 1999). Each fish was swum at 12, 14, 17, 22, and 26C, with at least 24 h between swimming trials. The order of test temperature at which fish were swum was randomly allocated (Hammill et al. 2004). The body length (mouth to caudal fin tip) of each fish was measured after swimming trials, and recovery MO2 measurements and Ucrit were corrected for body length (BL) and presented as BL s1. A fish was considered to be fatigued when it could no longer hold its position in the water column after a gentle prod with a plastic rod.
column88: highest swimming speed (Uf) + (time to fatigue/interval between speed increments) * speed increment (Ui)

During swimming trials, fish were individually contained in a restricted space (0.41 m long # 0.32 m wide # 0.70 m deep) within which laminar flow was approximated by a series of baffles. Unidirectional flow was produced by an electric outboard motor (Riptide RT40, Minn Kota, Mankato, MN), which was regulated with a variable DC power supply (MP3090, Powertech, Melbourne). Flow was proportional to the voltage output of the power sup- ply, and the power supply settings were calibrated using a flow probe (FP101, GlobalWater, Gold River, CA; sensitive to 0.01 m s1) so that voltage output could be related to water velocity in the restricted swimming space. The flume was situated in a temperature-controlled room, and water temperature was ad- ditionally regulated by two immersion heaters (Julabo Ther- momix, Seelbach, Germany). Fish were introduced into the flume enclosure for 10 min before experimen- tation to equilibrate body temperature to water temperature (Seebacher 1999). Each fish was swum at 12, 14, 17, 22, and 26C, with at least 24 h between swimming trials. The order of test temperature at which fish were swum was randomly allocated (Hammill et al. 2004). The body length (mouth to caudal fin tip) of each fish was measured after swimming trials, and recovery MO2 measurements and Ucrit were corrected for body length (BL) and presented as BL s1. A fish was considered to be fatigued when it could no longer hold its position in the water column after a gentle prod with a plastic rod.
column88: highest swimming speed (Uf) + (time to fatigue/interval between speed increments) * speed increment (Ui)

column76: We measured rates of MO2 at rest before swimming trials and during recovery immediately after swimming trials (i.e., recov- ery) using a standard closed respirometry technique (Cheung and Lam 1995; Sinclair et al. 2006). To determine resting met- abolic rates, fish were introduced into the respirometry cham- ber 20 min before measurements of MO2 were taken. During measurements, we observed that fish did not move and thereby confound measurements of resting MO2. Oxygen consumption was measured for periods of 15–25 min, depending on the test temperature. Metabolic scope was calculated as recovery MO2/ resting MO2.

column76: Burst-swimming performance was assessed by videotaping at least four swimming sequences for each individual at each temperature. Burst-swimming responses were elicited by placing adults in a swimming arena and tapping their dorsal surface with a ®ne probe, usually resulting in a C-start and several propulsive strokes <one startle response). Only startle responses from a stationary position that produced C-start responses were used in the analysis of burst swimming performance. Burst-swimming sequences were videotaped in a temperature controlled <M0.5°C) 1.00 m  ́ 0.40 m  ́ 0.25 m deep Perspex tank. Swimming responses were videotaped by recording the image at an angle of 90° above the arena using a ±1 video camera recording at 50 frames  was analysed to determine the maximum velocity <Umax distance moved throughout the initial 200 ms <D 200 taken to reach U max <T-Umax). We used a Hitachi video recorder <Model VT-L1000E) to play back the re- corded sequences frame by frame, with the image projected onto a 1.5 m  ́ 1.5 m screen. The approximate centre of mass of each ®sh <one-third the length of the total length) was manually digitised for each frame during a startle response, with the distance be- tween each mark measured. The start of a swimming sequence was deened as the frame immediately preceding the frame where movement was first detected, with the movement of the sh measured each frame for 300 ms. Velocity of the ®sh was deter mined by calculating the distance moved between each frame <i.e. 20 ms). The fastest of the swimming sequences analysed for each individual at each temperature was used as a measure of their maximum burst swimming performance.

Eggs were obtained from a ripe (eggs run with slight pressure) female caught in Lake Constance in May 1991 and fertilized by the dry method (cf. Craig, 1987 ) with the milt of two males. The egg strand was cut into subsamples of 76-125 eggs. Each subsample was first placed into a jar which stood in the baths of 10 or 12 oC, and then each jar was repeatedly transferred to the next bath with 2 oC higher or lower temperature at 5- 10 min. intervals until the final tem- perature was reached. When over 90% of the embryos had hatched, they were counted and expressed as a percent- age of the egg number counted previously, i.e. hatch rate. column76: Eggs from two females were pooled, fertilized in saline, and incubated at eight constant temperatures (8.5–26.8 °C, two replicates each) in aerated aquaria with stable oxygen, pH, and no ammonia detected. Temperatures were closely monitored and averaged across replicates. Development was tracked by noting key stages (eyed egg, beginning of hatching, 50% hatched, last hatch). Hatching success was measured as the proportion of normal larvae, and developmental advancement of hatched embryos was classified using Penaz & Gajdusek’s (1979) scheme (steps VI–VIII).
column107: Fish were induced to develop gametes by a series of injections with common carp pituitary extract and human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) (Kucharczyk et al., 1997), at total dose of 4.0 mg kg–1 with 2200 IU kg–1 and 2.0 mg kg–1 with 1100 IU kg–1, for females and males respectively. Milt was collected from ten males and eggs from two females. The quality of sperm was expressed as the percentage of motile spermatozoa by microscopic (500 X) observation of sperm activated with 0.5% NaCl (Babiak et al., 1995). Only samples with 80% (or more) motile spermatozoa were pooled and used in fertilization. Females were stripped of eggs 14 hours after the last injection.

column76: Oxygen consumption rates were measured for groups of schooling fish (n = 6–25) instead of individuals, because individually separated clupeids are hyperactive, lose scales and die due to stress (Hettler 1976; Blaxter and Hunter 1982). At the end of an experiment, fish were removed and rapidly killed by an overdose of anaesthetic (MS-222) and weighed individually (0.001 g accuracy). After fish were transferred into the respirometer chamber, they firstly showed very high oxygen consumption due to handling stress, i.e. acclimation phase. This initial phase was not included in the data analysis. The separation between acclimation and routine phase followed the procedure of Herrmann and Enders (2000). For calculations of metabolic rates, only data of the routine phase were used. Taking into account the chamber volume and the displaced volume of the fish, the actual oxygen uptake rate in one measuring interval in mgO2 h-1 of the fish group was calculated by linear regression of oxygen concentration on time. Only oxygen consumption rates with a regression coefficient [0.9 times the average of all regression coef- ficients (*0.97) were selected to calculate metabolic rates (Herrmann and Enders 2000). The total oxygen uptake was then divided by numbers of fish and fish wet weight after values for bacterial respiration were subtracted. Standard metabolism (RS) was calculated as the median of the lower 10% of the respiration rates in the routine phase over one experiment (Herrmann and Enders 2000). For the calculation of routine metabolism (RR), all oxygen consumption values of the routine phase have been used

After fish were transferred into the respirometer chamber, they firstly showed very high oxygen consumption due to handling stress, i.e. acclimation phase. This initial phase was not included in the data analysis. The separation between acclimation and routine phase followed the procedure of Herrmann and Enders (2000). For calculations of metabolic rates, only data of the routine phase were used. Taking into account the chamber volume and the displaced volume of the fish, the actual oxygen uptake rate in one measuring interval in mgO2 h-1 of the fish group was calculated by linear regression of oxygen concentration on time. Only oxygen consumption rates with a regression coefficient [0.9 times the average of all regression coef- ficients (*0.97) were selected to calculate metabolic rates (Herrmann and Enders 2000). The total oxygen uptake was then divided by numbers of fish and fish wet weight after values for bacterial respiration were subtracted. Standard metabolism (RS) was calculated as the median of the lower 10% of the respiration rates in the routine phase over one experiment (Herrmann and Enders 2000). For the calculation of routine metabolism (RR), all oxygen consumption values of the routine phase have been used

column76: Oxygen consumption was quantified as part of a series of seven sequential temperature‐exposure trials conducted between 14 August and 24 September 2005. All fish were initially acclimated to 16 °C for three weeks before experimentation began. Each trial lasted six days and exposed fish to a fixed test temperature that increased by 2 °C increments across trials (18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28 °C), except the final trial, which used 27 °C due to mortality at 28 °C. At the start of each trial, fish from two age classes (0+ and 2+) were randomly assigned to individual respirometers. For each age class, treatment fish were held in a tank system in which water temperature was increased to the target test temperature, while control fish remained at 16 °C.  All respirometers initially operated as open, flow-through systems. Once fish were placed inside, test-system water was gradually warmed by 2 °C over 2 h to reach the trial’s experimental temperature. Pre-measurement conditions - Behavioural monitoring occurred from days 1–3, after which fish were food-deprived for 42 h to ensure a postabsorptive state (avoiding digestion-related increases in metabolic rate). Oxygen consumption measurements began at 11:00 on day 5. For oxygen measurements, the respirometers were switched from flow-through to closed systems. Oxygen concentrations inside each chamber were recorded for a minimum of 90 minutes for individual fish.
column88:
O2 consumed = [(deltaO2) - BODblanks) * V*(60T^-1)]/W
Where DeltaO2) was the difference between the final oxygen level in the respirometer and the initial level (mg L)1), BOD (mg L)1) was biological (microbial) respiration once the fish was removed, V was the volume of the container (5Æ7 L for 0+ and 11Æ3 L for 2+ Atlantic salmon), T was the duration of the measurement (min) and W was the wet weight of the fish (grams). The volume of the respirometer was not adjusted for the volume of the fish.

column76: Oxygen consumption (Mo₂) was measured using automated intermittent-flow respirometry in temperature-controlled water baths. Each respirometer had two loops: a closed loop with an oxygen sensor that logged dissolved oxygen every 2 seconds, and a flush loop used to replenish oxygen so levels stayed above 80% saturation. Metabolic rate was calculated only during the closed periods, because that’s when the fish’s breathing is the only thing causing oxygen to drop. RMR calculation -- Because the two study sites used different protocols, all minimum metabolic rates were standardized as RMR. Lake Victoria fish underwent a chase protocol and required a longer recovery, so RMR was calculated from the lowest 10% of Mo₂ values collected during a 9-hour post-exercise period, excluding outliers. Lake Nabugabo fish were transferred into chambers without chasing and recovered more quickly, but only two low, stable Mo₂ values were available. Recovery tests (Nyboer & Chapman 2017) showed that Nile perch reached baseline metabolism after ~180 min post-chase and ~140 min post-transfer. To ensure comparability across lakes, only Mo₂ measurements taken after 140 minutes were used for RMR calculations in both datasets. For Lake Nabugabo fish, this corresponded to the two measurements collected after this threshold.

column76: Oxygen consumption (Mo₂) was measured using automated intermittent-flow respirometry in temperature-controlled water baths. Each respirometer had two loops: a closed loop with an oxygen sensor that logged dissolved oxygen every 2 seconds, and a flush loop used to replenish oxygen so levels stayed above 80% saturation. Metabolic rate was calculated only during the closed periods, because that’s when the fish’s breathing is the only thing causing oxygen to drop. RMR calculation -- Because the two study sites used different protocols, all minimum metabolic rates were standardized as RMR. Lake Victoria fish underwent a chase protocol and required a longer recovery, so RMR was calculated from the lowest 10% of Mo₂ values collected during a 9-hour post-exercise period, excluding outliers. Lake Nabugabo fish were transferred into chambers without chasing and recovered more quickly, but only two low, stable Mo₂ values were available. Recovery tests (Nyboer & Chapman 2017) showed that Nile perch reached baseline metabolism after ~180 min post-chase and ~140 min post-transfer. To ensure comparability across lakes, only Mo₂ measurements taken after 140 minutes were used for RMR calculations in both datasets. For Lake Nabugabo fish, this corresponded to the two measurements collected after this threshold.

column76: fish respirometry chambers the night before experiments to ensure post-absorptive status. Chambers were submerged in a temperature-controlled, aerated 300-L fiberglass tank set to each fish’s acclimation temperature, with black plastic sheeting used to minimize disturbance. Dissolved oxygen was maintained >95% saturation using air stones and, at warm temperatures, a wet-dry trickle column. Resting metabolic rate (RMR) was measured using intermittent respirometry, with alternating flush and sealed measurement periods. During each sealed period, water samples were taken at the start and end to determine PO₂ using a polarographic electrode; O₂ concentrations (mg O₂ L⁻¹) were calculated using established nomograms. Three measurement periods were completed per fish, and mean O₂ decline was used to calculate RMR. After trials, fish mass and length were recorded. RMR was expressed as a mass-independent rate, scaled using a 0.79 mass exponent.

column76: Fish were anesthetized, weighed, and placed in a well-aerated bath with their gills continuously irrigated. ECG electrodes were placed on the heart to record heart rate. Heart rate was stimulated with injections of atropine and isoproterenol and allowed to stabilize for ~20 minutes. Water temperature was gradually increased or decreased in steps until the fish showed heart rhythm problems or the bath started to freeze. the maximum heart rate and its temperature, and the temperature where the heart became arrhythmic. Heart rate data were analyzed using segmented regression to find points where heart function was affected by temperature.

column76: Maximum daily consumption was measured by feeding northern squawfish ad libitum on juvenile salmonids over a 48-hour period at controlled temperatures. Only healthy, active fish were used. Fish were fasted long enough to empty their stomachs, using temperature-specific gut evacuation equations. Groups were stratified into weight classes. Fish were fed juvenile Chinook and Coho salmon to satiation. Feeding occurred  at the start of the trial then every 4 hours (total of 14 feedings). Final feeding at hour 47.5. Final body weight of each predator was measured with stomach contents removed (±1 g). Maximum daily ration was calculated as: (Total prey consumed in centigrams) / (Total predator mass in grams) / 24 h reported as cg·g⁻¹·day⁻¹

column102: *fish "were collected and maintained as described by van der Lingen (1994)". I consulted this paper to get the info. Citation: Van Der Lingen, C. (1994). Effect of particle size and concentration on the feeding behaviour of adult pilchard Sardinops sagax. Marine Ecology Progress Series, 109, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.3354/meps109001. ALSO, the authors reported results from 19 experiments, and the data presented in the graph (swimming speed vs temp) are inextricable -- impossible to say which point represents which experiment and what the conditions were. While they list 'initial temperatures' used, the temperatures I extracted from the graph do not match those values. I used mine, rounded to the nearest hundredth. n_temps was estimated by counting unique rounded whole# temp values from extraction (which were 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 22 = 12 temps). Also, acclimation time was unclear -- when experiments were done at temperatures other than ambient, the fish were habituated for at least 4 days to the test temp. Because of this short amount of time, I put curve type as acute-change. Also, sample sizes were unclear, as well as whether the same fish were used for each experiment (the authors say there were 10 fish, but some weren't considered for swimming speeds, and under figure 2, they wrote n = 117). So, for sample size and cohort_ID --> n/a. There was data on the size of the 10 fish, so size data refers to n = 10.

column76: Experiments occurred between October 16, 2012, and November 5, 2013, at ambient water temperatures (20.7–30.3 °C), thereby permitting us to define variation in swimming performance and metabolic scope across different water temperatures and seasons. Water temperature was kept as constant as possible during the protocol for any one fish (range=0.4–1.5 °C). Additional experiments were performed during the summer at adjusted higher temperatures. Heaters were used to gradually increase water temperatures during overnight swim tunnel acclimations to a maximum of ~6 °C above ambient to extend the temperature range (Lee et al. 2003). Adjusted treatment temperatures ranged between 30 and 36 °C to stay below bonefish CTmax of 37.9 °C (Murchie et al. 2011a).
column107: Water changes were performed periodically (approximately every 5 min) en route back to the facility using protocols described by Murchie et al. (2009). Fish were given a minimum of 24 h to acclimate to laboratory conditions before experimentation

column76: Indi- vidual fish were placed into 27.5×17.5 cm plastic aquaria (hereafter, ‘arenas’) housed in a recirculating water bath after they were measured in mm TL and weighed to the nearest 0.01 g (Table 1). To prevent fish from seeing other individuals during the trail, the sides of the arenas were painted black. A recirculating chiller or submersible heater was used to maintain the water temperature in the water bath appropriate for the temperature treatment being tested. Each arena was kept aerated while housing fish. Arenas were placed over a 2 cm × 2 cm grid on a white background. Fish were habit- uated to the arenas for 7 days and fed a ration of frozen bloodworms each day during this period. Fish were fasted for 48 h before we stationed a GoPro® camera above each individual arena, capturing the entire arena in the field of view. The aerator was removed from the arena during video recording to prevent agitation of the water’s surface. Fish were recorded continuously for 15 min (Gautrias et al., 2009; Troia et al., 2016). We discarded the first 5 min of video to account for fish potentially being disturbed when the camera was turned on. Activity was quantified from the subsequent 10 min of video by randomly selecting a subsample of 10 non- overlapping 30-s intervals during the filmed trail and calculat- ing the average number of 2 cm × 2 cm grids the fish traversed per unit time. All 12 fish belonging to a single acclimation temperature were filmed on the same day, beginning at 0900 h and finishing within 2 h. During filming trials, we recorded two fish concurrently using different cameras. Filming for all five acclimation treatments was completed in 5 days.

A recirculating chiller or submersible heater was used to maintain the water temperature in the water bath appropriate for the temperature treatment being tested. Each arena was kept aerated while housing fish. Arenas were placed over a 2 cm × 2 cm grid on a white background. Fish were habit- uated to the arenas for 7 days and fed a ration of frozen bloodworms each day during this period. Fish were fasted for 48 h before we stationed a GoPro® camera above each individual arena, capturing the entire arena in the field of view. Activity was quantified from the subsequent 10 min of video by randomly selecting a subsample of 10 non- overlapping 30-s intervals during the filmed trail and calculat- ing the average number of 2 cm × 2 cm grids the fish traversed per unit time. column76: We used a 5-L swim tunnel respirometer (Loligo Systems, Tjele, Denmark) to carry out swimming performance trials (Svendsen et al., 2015). We included eight dace and eight stonerollers in each of five temperature treatments (10, 15, 20, 25 and 30◦ C; total n = 80). We used either submersible heaters or ice packs to maintain water temperature in the swim tunnel within0.2◦Cofthetemperaturetreatmentbeingtested.Trials of critical swimming velocity (Ucrit) were conducted using a velocity increment based on the total length (TL) of the fish (Brett, 1964; Morozov et al., 2018). Before being introduced to the swim chamber, individual fish were measured in mm TL and weighed to the nearest 0.01 g (Table 1). To discourage the fish from attempting to rest against the back screen of the swim chamber, we placed a partitioning shade over the front half of the chamber and shined light at the back of the chamber. Following methods for other fish species, fish were first acclimated to the chamber with no flow velocity for 30 min (Lehman et al., 2017) and then for 10 min at a water velocity of 1 TL s−1 before beginning the experiment. Swimming trials began at a water velocity of 2 TL s−1, with velocity being increased by 1 increment (1 TL) every 5 min and ending once the fish was fatigued (Nelson et al., 2003). Fatigue was determined as the velocity at which the fish became pinned to the back of the swim tunnel and would not return to swimming after visual or acoustic stimuli.

column76: Burst swimming responses were assessed in a 35 × 24 × 4 cm aquarium with a 20 cm measuring tape placed in the field of view for calibration. The aquarium was secured inside an arena made of plywood and a mirror angled at 45°. A Panasonic Lumix DMC-TZ40 camera recorded the image at 100 frames per second off the mirror. Burst swimming responses were elicited by gently tapping the fish’s tail using a metal rod when fish were motionless on the bottom of the tank. Instantaneous swimming speed was extracted from videos using KINOVEA© [experimental version 0.8.25-x64 (http://www.kinovea.org)]. Only swimming responses where the fish exhibited a C-start escape response were analysed. The point between the eyes of each fish was digitised to ensure a consistent point was tracked. A minimum of three burst responses was recorded for each fish and the maximum instantaneous speed for each escape response was determined. The maximum instantaneous speeds for each fish were averaged at each test temperature and used in statistical analysis.

column76: We quantified the maximum ventilation and metabolic rate of each individual fish at 15 °C, 22 °C, 28 °C, 33 °C, and 36 °C (and 12 °C for ventilation rate only) in a randomised order. We tested maximum ventilation rate by chasing a fish (with a hand net) for a minute to elicit a sustained escape response. Fish were then immediately placed into a transparent petri dish and filmed ventrally for 60 s using a Panasonic Lumix DMC-TZ40 camera at a rate of 100 frames per second. Ventilation rate was then determined by visually counting the number of operculum ventilations over 60 s. Immediately after ventilation rate was filmed, fish were placed in a 133 mL respirometer with a magnetic stirrer that produced a current within the respirometer for the fish to swim against (the current was turned up until fish could just maintain forward movement within the water column) to assess maximum metabolic rate. A PreSens Fibox 4 (POF-L2.5-1) with a polymer optical fiber and oxygen minisensor spots (batch ID—140117-001) was used to measure percentage air saturation (% a.s.) (one measurement/second) within the respirometer over 5 min of testing. After individual fish were tested, they were then placed in an oxygen-saturated recovery bucket where the water temperature changed at a rate of 3 °C/h to bring the fish back to their treatment conditions. Three control (no fish) water samples were taken at each test temperature over 5 min to assess for any oxygen consumption or production within the bottle during testing.

column76: Burst swimming speed was assessed to gain a whole- organism measure of performance capacity at all test temperatures (see detailed methods in Seebacher et al. 2014). Fish were placed in an 8 cm 9 10 cm testing aquarium with a fixed 10-cm measuring tape placed in the field of view for calibration. A high-speed camera (Pana- sonic Lumix DMC-TZ40) was set up directly above the middle of the testing aquarium and recorded the image. Burst swimming responses were promoted by tapping next to the fish’s tail using a thin metal rod when fish were stationary. A minimum of three burst responses was recorded for each fish, and the maximum instantaneous speed for each escape response was determined and extracted from videos using the program KINOVAÓ (ex- perimental version 0.8.25-x64). Only swimming responses where the fish exhibited a C-start escape response (pow- erful escape response where fish bends body into C shape to flick tail for rapid burst movement) were analysed. We digitised the point between the eyes of each fish to ensure consistent tracking. Maximum instantaneous speeds for individual fish were averaged at each acute test temperature.

column76: Routine metabolic rate was assessed prior to burst swimming speed to minimise stress and to reduce error in metabolic rate samples. Fish were placed in darkened (black plastic covered) 350-mL respirometers for 1 h within a water bath set at the daily test temperature prior to the start of testing to allow the fish’s metabolic rates to stabilise. Oxygen consumption was then measured in the following hour using a PreSens Fibox 4 (POF-L2.5-1). A polymer optical fibre and oxygen minisensor spots (batch ID—140117-001) were used to measure the decrease in per cent air saturation within the respirometer. Control measures were taken from respirometers full of sea water (no fish) to detect for any microorganism metabolic activity or oxygen production occurring within the testing water that may affect results.

column53: each point represents the percentage of normal developing larvae (NDL) calculated per tank (i.e., per replicate), at a given incubation temperature. For each temperature, they incubated replicate tanks (typically 6 per temperature, except 4 at 9°C). There were about 100 eggs in each tank
column76: Egg veils were collected from coastal waters using a scoop net and transported to the lab. The egg veils were cut into ~2–3 cm squares, each containing about 100 eggs. Egg pieces were placed into small tanks (500 mL) filled with artificial seawater (salinity 32–33). Incubation was performed at six different temperatures: 9°C, 13°C, 15°C, 18°C, 21°C, and 24°C. Water temperature was adjusted gradually before incubation began. twice daily, hatched larvae and dead embryos were counted. Hatched larvae were preserved in ethanol for assessment. Deformities were checked under a stereomicroscope. Deformed larvae showed issues like bent or stunted notochords or jaws. Percentage of NDL (normal developing larvae, i.e., non-deformed live larvae) to the total collected individuals was calculated.

column76: The maximum level of oxygen consumption observed after strenuous swimming activity by cod was taken as a measure of their active metabolic rate.   Unfed acclimated fish were chased witha net inside a large tank until they refused to move or to show any further response to the net. column53: eggs were divided into pools of 60–130 from each cross  and incubated in Petri dishes (2–6 Petri dishes per temperature and  cross)
column76: Eggs from each cross were pooled (60–130 per pool) and incubated in Petri dishes (2–6 per temperature) with dechlorinated water and a fungicide, across temperatures from 15–36 °C (3 °C increments) under a 12L:12D cycle. Water was changed daily, with brief air exposure to trigger hatching when embryos reached stages 32–36. Dishes were checked twice daily for embryo viability and hatching. Hatched larvae were euthanized, fixed in formalin, and stored in ethanol at 4 °C for later analysis.
column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. In spring 2021, males and females were placed in separate tanks and gradually induced into spawning by increasing temperature and photoperiod. After 3 weeks on a rich diet, gametes were collected in vitro from 20 females and 10 males per population. Eggs and milt from each population were pooled, mixed, and fertilized in Petri dishes. Four crosses were produced: northern, southern, and reciprocal hybrids (N♀×S♂ and S♀×N♂). I am only using data from northern and southern crosses--no reciprocol

column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. column107: Adult Fundulus heteroclitus were collected in 2019 from New Hampshire (north) and Georgia (south) and acclimated at UBC under controlled conditions. column76: In 2012, creek side repeat swimming performance tests were conducted on a subset of juvenile Arctic char (smolts) over the range of naturally occurring temperatures to assess the effect of temperature on cardiorespiratory performance.  90 L swim tunnel respirometer with a 70 × 20 × 20 cm test section (Loligo). A small electrical charge (<6 V) was applied to the rear gate of the test section to motivate fish to swim. Fish were allowed to acclimate at a low water speed (0.5 body lengths/s; bl/s) for 30 min after which the speed was increased by 0.5 bl/s every 10 min until the fish fatigued and was not able to remove itself from the rear gate within 5 s. Fish were then allowed to recover for 30 min at 0.5 bl/s and were then given a second swim test except speed was increased every 1 min rather than every 10 min. The 30-min recovery time was intentionally shorter than previous studies (Jain et al., 1998; MacNutt, Hinch, Farrell, & Topp, 2004) to assess the capacity of the fish to recover rapidly. The short step length in the second test was selected (Farrell, 2008) as a rapid assessment of recovery in order to limit the duration of the static temperature expo- sure and increase throughput under time constraints in the field. The Brett equation (Brett, 1964) was used to calculate the critical swimming speed for each test (test 1: Umax1; test 2: Umax2) and the quotient of (recovery ratio; RR) and difference between these values were considered measures of recovery (Jain et al., 1998).
